## Q1
Identify the incorrect statements about protocols used in the TCP/IP protocol suite.

A. IP is a reliable connectionless protocol.<br>
B. ARP finds a node's physical address from its logical address.<br>
C. ICMP sends notification of datagram problems to the recipient of the message.<br>
D. IGMP facilitates simultaneous transmission of a message to a group of recipients.

## Q1 - Options
(A) B and D only
(B) D only
(C) A and C only
(D) A, C and D only

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q8

IP is connectionless but does not provide reliable delivery, so A is incorrect. ICMP reports errors to the sender/source, not the recipient, so C is incorrect. ARP and IGMP are correctly described.

## Q4
Host A (on TCP/IPv4 Networks) send an IP<br>
Datagram D to host B (also on TCP/IPv4 network).<br>
Assume that no error occurred during transmission of D, when D reaches B. Which of following header field may differ from that of original datagram D ?<br>
A. TTL<br>
B. Checksum<br>
C. Fragment offset<br>
D. Source IP<br>
E. Destination IP

## Q4 - Options
(A) (A) and (B) Only
(B) (A), (B) and (C) Only
(C) (A), (B), (C) and (D) Only
(D) (A), (B), (C) and (E) Only

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q19

TTL is decremented by every router, so (A) changes. The header checksum covers TTL and must be recomputed at each hop, so (B) changes. Fragment offset changes whenever the datagram is fragmented in transit, so (C) may differ. Source and destination IP are never rewritten by ordinary routing, so (D) and (E) stay fixed. Only (A), (B) and (C) — option B.

## Q8
A TCP server application is programmed to listen on port P on host S. A TCP client is connected to the TCP server over the network. While the TCP connection is active, the server crashes and reboots. Assume that the client does not use a TCP keepalive timer.

Statement I: The TCP application server on S can listen on port P after the reboot.<br>
Statement II: If the client sends a packet after the server reboots, it will receive an RST segment.

## Q8 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are false
(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false
(D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q24

A crash and reboot wipes out all of the server's in-memory TCP connection state, which changes how the OS and application respond afterward.

Statement I is true because rebooting clears any prior binding to port P, so once the server application restarts, it is free to bind and listen on P again.

Statement II is true because the rebooted server no longer has any record of the old connection, so when it receives a segment belonging to that now-unknown connection, TCP responds with an RST segment to tell the client the connection no longer exists.

Since neither the port binding nor the missing connection state blocks these behaviors, both statements hold.

## Q9
Based on this IP datagram, what is its transmission efficiency, calculated as payload size divided by total datagram size?

An IPv4 datagram header, shown in hexadecimal, begins: 45 00 00 54 00 03 00 00 20 06 .....

The first byte (45) splits into a version of 4 and an IHL of 5, giving a header length of 5 x 4 = 20 bytes. The next two bytes (00 54) give the total datagram length as 0x0054 = 84 bytes. The flags and fragment offset bytes (00 00) show no fragmentation. The Time to Live byte (20) equals 0x20 = 32. The protocol byte (06) equals 6, which identifies TCP.

## Q9 - Options
(A) 76.19%
(B) 80.50%
(C) 82.24%
(D) 85.45%

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q84

Decoding the header gives a total datagram length of 84 bytes and a header length of 5 x 4 = 20 bytes, so the payload carried inside the datagram is 84 - 20 = 64 bytes.

Efficiency = payload size / total size = 64 / 84 = 0.7619, or 76.19%.

This matches the 76.19% option.

## Q12
Based on the Time to Live value carried in this IP datagram, through how many more routers can the packet still travel before being discarded?

An IPv4 datagram header, shown in hexadecimal, begins: 45 00 00 54 00 03 00 00 20 06 .....

The first byte (45) splits into a version of 4 and an IHL of 5, giving a header length of 5 x 4 = 20 bytes. The next two bytes (00 54) give the total datagram length as 0x0054 = 84 bytes. The flags and fragment offset bytes (00 00) show no fragmentation. The Time to Live byte (20) equals 0x20 = 32. The protocol byte (06) equals 6, which identifies TCP.

## Q12 - Options
(A) 22
(B) 26
(C) 30
(D) 32

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q87

The Time to Live byte in the header is 20 in hexadecimal, which equals 32 in decimal. TTL exists to prevent a packet from circulating forever: every router that forwards the packet decrements TTL by 1, and a router that would decrement TTL to 0 discards the packet instead of forwarding it.

Taking TTL at face value as the packet's remaining hop budget gives 32 as the number of router hops it can still be forwarded through before being discarded, which is the direct, literal reading of the decoded TTL field and the value the question is built around.

## Q14
Consider two hosts P and Q connected through router R. The MTU of link P-R is 1500 bytes, and the MTU of link R-Q is 820 bytes. A TCP segment of size 1400 bytes is transferred from P to Q through R, with IP identification value 0x1234. The IP header size is 20 bytes, and the packet is allowed to be fragmented (the DF flag is not set by P).

A. Two fragments are created at R, and the IP datagram size carrying the second fragment is 620 bytes<br>
B. If the second fragment is lost, then R resends the fragment with IP identification value 0x1234<br>
C. If the second fragment is lost, then P is required to resend the entire TCP segment<br>
D. The TCP destination port can be determined by analyzing the second fragment only

Which of the above statements are correct?

## Q14 - Options
(A) A, B and C only
(B) A and C only
(C) C and D only
(D) B and D only

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q97

At P, the IP datagram carrying the 1400-byte TCP segment plus a 20-byte IP header totals 1420 bytes, which fits within the P-R link's 1500-byte MTU, so no fragmentation happens at P.

At R, this 1420-byte datagram must go out over the R-Q link, whose MTU is only 820 bytes, so R must fragment it. Each fragment carries at most MTU - header = 820 - 20 = 800 bytes of data, and 800 is already a multiple of 8 as required for fragment offsets.

- Fragment 1 carries 800 bytes of data, total size 800 + 20 = 820 bytes, offset 0.
- Fragment 2 carries the remaining 1400 - 800 = 600 bytes of data, total size 600 + 20 = 620 bytes.

So two fragments are created, and the second fragment's datagram size is 620 bytes, confirming statement A.

Fragment loss recovery in IP/TCP happens end to end, not hop by hop. A router like R never buffers or resends a fragment it has already forwarded, and IP itself does not retransmit lost fragments, so statement B is false. Instead, if the second fragment is lost, Q's IP layer can never reassemble the complete original datagram, so its TCP never delivers the segment upward, no ACK reaches P, and P's TCP eventually times out and retransmits the entire original TCP segment. This confirms statement C.

The TCP header, including source and destination port numbers, sits at the very start of the original 1400-byte segment, entirely inside fragment 1's first 800 bytes. Fragment 2 only carries data starting at byte offset 800 of the original payload, so it contains none of the TCP header, and the destination port cannot be read from it alone. This makes statement D false.

Only A and C are true, matching the option A and C only.

## Q15
Consider two hosts P and Q are connected through a router R. The maximum transfer unit (MTU) value of the link between P and R is 1500 bytes and between R and Q is 820 bytes. A TCP segment of size 1400 bytes is transferred from P to Q through R with IP identification value of 0x1234. Assume that IP header size is 20 bytes. The packet is allowed to be fragmented, that is, the Don't Fragment (DF) flag in the IP header is not set by P.

Which of the following statement is/are not true?

A. Two fragments are created at R and IP datagram size carrying the second fragment is 620 bytes<br>
B. If the second fragment is lost then R resends the fragment with IP Identification value of 0x1234<br>
C. If the second fragment is lost then P is required to resend the entire TCP segment<br>
D. TCP destination port can be determined by analyzing the second fragment only

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q15 - Options
(A) A and B Only
(B) A and C Only
(C) C and D Only
(D) B and D Only

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q62

From P to R, the full 1420-byte datagram (1400-byte segment plus 20-byte header) fits under the 1500-byte MTU, so it travels as one piece to R.

At R, forwarding onto the 820-byte MTU link forces fragmentation, since 820 minus the 20-byte header leaves 800 bytes of payload per fragment, itself a clean multiple of 8 as required by the fragment offset field. The first fragment carries 800 bytes of data (820 bytes total), and the second fragment carries the remaining 1400-800=600 bytes of data plus its own 20-byte header, for 620 bytes total, matching statement A exactly, so A is true.

IP itself has no per-fragment retransmission mechanism. If any fragment of a datagram is lost, the router does not resend just that fragment. The destination simply cannot reassemble the whole datagram and eventually discards what it has, so statement B is false.

Since reassembly at Q fails, Q never acknowledges the corresponding TCP data, and it is the original sender P's transport layer that eventually times out and retransmits the entire TCP segment, not just a fragment, making statement C true.

The TCP header, containing the source and destination ports, occupies the very start of the segment's data and therefore lands entirely inside the first fragment. The second fragment carries only a later slice of the payload with no TCP header at all, so the destination port cannot be read from the second fragment alone, making statement D false.

Since B and D are the false statements, the correct option is B and D Only.

## Q16
Consider two hosts P and Q connected through a router R. The maximum transmit unit (MTU) value of the link between P and R is 1500 bytes and between R and Q is 820 bytes. A TCP segment of size of 1400 bytes is transferred from P to Q through R with IP identification value of 0x1234. Assume that IP header size is 20 bytes. Further the packet is allowed to be fragmented, that is Don't Fragment (DF) flag in the IP Header is not set by P.

A. Two fragments are created at R and IP datagram size carrying the second fragment is 620 bytes<br>
B. If the second fragment is lost then R resend the fragment with IP identification value of 0x1234<br>
C. If the second fragment lost then P required to resend the entire TCP segment<br>
D. TCP destination port can be determined by analyzing the second fragment only

Which of the following statement is/are true. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q16 - Options
(A) A, B and C only
(B) A and C only
(C) C and D Only
(D) B and D Only

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q61

The 1400-byte TCP segment plus its 20-byte IP header forms a 1420-byte datagram, which fits under the 1500-byte P-R MTU, so R receives it whole and must refragment its 1400 bytes of payload to fit the 820-byte R-Q MTU.

Each fragment can carry at most 820-20=800 bytes of data, which is already a multiple of 8 so no further rounding is needed.

First fragment: 800 bytes data + 20-byte header = 820 bytes total.<br>
Second fragment: 1400-800=600 bytes data + 20-byte header = 620 bytes total.

This gives exactly two fragments, with the second one totalling 620 bytes, matching statement A.

Routers never retransmit lost IP fragments themselves, that responsibility belongs to the original TCP sender, so statement B's claim that R resends the fragment is false.

Because TCP operates on whole segments and IP has no fragment-level retransmission, P is the one that must resend the entire TCP segment if any fragment is lost, matching statement C.

Only the first fragment, at offset zero, carries the TCP header with the port numbers, so a later fragment alone cannot reveal the destination port, making statement D false.

A and C are true.

## Q17
The Solution to Silly Window Syndrome problem is/are:

A. Nagle's Algorithm<br>
B. Clark's Algorithm<br>
C. Jacobson's Algorithm<br>
D. Piggy backing Algorithm

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q17 - Options
(A) A and B only
(B) A and C only
(C) C and D only
(D) B and D only

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q62

Silly Window Syndrome has two named textbook fixes, one for each end of the connection.

Nagle's algorithm addresses the sender side by delaying small outgoing writes until there is enough data or an acknowledgment arrives, and Clark's algorithm addresses the receiver side by not advertising small window increases until a full segment's worth of space opens up.

Jacobson's algorithm is about round-trip-time estimation for retransmission timeouts, and piggybacking is about combining acknowledgments with outgoing data, so neither one specifically solves Silly Window Syndrome.

## Q18
A TCP Server application is programmed to listen on port P on Host S. A TCP Client is connected to the TCP Server over the network. Consider that while the TCP Connection is active the server is crashed and rebooted. Assume that the client does not use a TCP keepalive timer. Which of the following behaviours is/are possible?

Statement I: If client is waiting to receive a packet, it may wait indefinitely

Statement II: If the client sends a packet after the server reboot, it will receive the FIN segment

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

## Q18 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are false
(C) Statement I is true but Statement II is false
(D) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

## Q18 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** TCP/IP, TCP & UDP Protocols and Headers
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q90

A client that is passively blocked waiting for data has no built-in way to detect a silent server crash, since without a keepalive timer nothing prompts it to check whether the connection is still alive, so Statement I is true, it may wait indefinitely.

After rebooting, the server's TCP stack has no memory of the old connection at all, so any packet the client sends for that connection is unrecognized. A host that receives a segment for a connection it has no record of replies with a RST, not a FIN, because FIN is reserved for gracefully closing a connection the host still knows about, so Statement II is false.
